correlation-s1.title: Study time and quiz scores
correlation-s1.text: A teacher records how many hours each of 8 students studied for a quiz and their score out of 100. (Invented data.)

plot.label: Scatterplot of 8 students: hours studied, 1 to 6, against quiz score, 62 to 86, rising in a fairly tight straight band

correlation-s2.title: Four scatterplots
correlation-s2.text: Each plot shows 20 points of invented data, with its correlation computed from the data printed above it.

items.q: Use technology to find the correlation $r$ between hours studied and quiz score. Give three decimal places.

why.correct: Technology (a linear regression or correlation command on the two lists) gives $r = 0.951$.

mistakes.why: The sign is wrong: scores rise with study time, so the correlation is positive.

why.correct: $r$ gives direction (sign) and strength (closeness to 1 or $-1$) of a linear association.
options: Correlation measures a linear association, not accuracy.
$r$ is not a percent of students, and it says nothing about cause.
Right: $r$ near 1 means a strong positive linear association.
That would be a slope. $r$ has no units and does not measure change per hour.
The quiz scores are about 95% accurate measures
About 95% of the students scored higher because they studied more
A strong, positive, linear link between study time and score
Each extra hour of study raises the score by 0.95 points

items.q: The teacher recomputes $r$ with study time in minutes instead of hours. What happens to $r$?

why.correct: $r$ is unitless: it does not change when either variable changes units.
options: Rescaling a variable does not change how tightly the points follow a line.
Right: changing units changes every z-score not at all, so $r$ is unchanged.
Any units work; $r$ is based on standardized values.
$r$ is always between $-1$ and 1; it has no units to convert.
It becomes 60 times smaller, 0.016
It stays 0.95
It can no longer be computed
It becomes 60 times larger, 57.0

items.q: If quiz score were put on the horizontal axis and hours on the vertical axis, what would the correlation be?

options: Switching axes does not reverse the direction: high scores still go with more hours.
Right: $r$ treats the two variables the same way, so switching them leaves it unchanged.
A correlation can never exceed 1, and switching axes leaves it as it was.
Correlation does not depend on which variable is called explanatory.
The negative, $-0.95$
The same, 0.95
The reciprocal, 1.05
Zero, since a score is unable to explain hours

items.q: A ninth student studied 6 hours but scored 40. What would adding this student do to $r$?

why.correct: Like the mean and SD, $r$ is pulled by outliers.
options: The new point sits far below the trend, so the association gets weaker, not stronger.
Right: with the ninth point, technology gives $r = 0.14$. Correlation is not resistant to outliers.
It drops a lot, to about 0.14, but the other eight points still trend upward.
One point far from the line can change $r$ a lot. Correlation is not resistant.
It would rise, since the new student studied a lot
It would drop sharply, to about 0.14: $r$ is not resistant
It would become negative, since 40 is the lowest score
It would barely change, since one point out of nine is small

items.q: Which plot shows a strong relationship even though its correlation is close to 0?

why.correct: Correlation near 0 means no linear association; there may still be a strong curved one.
options: Its $r$ is close to 1, not 0.
Those points are widely scattered; the relationship really is weak.
Its $r$ is far from 0.
Right: the points follow an arch very closely, but $r$ measures only linear association, and an arch is not a line.
The strong positive plot, $r = 0.99$
The weak positive plot, $r = 0.29$
The moderate negative plot, $r = -0.79$
The curved plot, $r = 0.04$

items.q: Which plot has the strongest linear association?

why.correct: Linear strength is the size of $r$, $|r|$, whatever its sign.
options: Wide spread means a weak association.
Right: its $r$ is closest to 1 or $-1$ in size, and its points hug a line.
The curve is clear, but it is not linear, and $r$ measures linear strength.
The sign gives direction only. Compare sizes: 0.99 is larger than 0.79.
The plot with $r = 0.29$, because its points spread widest
The plot with $r = 0.99$
The plot with $r = 0.04$, because its pattern is clear
The plot with $r = -0.79$, because negative is stronger

items.q: What does the plot with $r = -0.79$ show?

why.correct: Sign: direction. Size: strength of the linear pattern.
options: A negative $r$ is not weaker; $-0.79$ is as strong as 0.79.
That would be a slope; $r$ has no units.
$r$ is not a percent of points.
Right: the negative sign gives the direction, and a size of 0.79 is a moderate linear association, close to strong.
A weak association, because $r$ is negative
That $y$ decreases by 0.79 for each unit of $x$
That 79% of the points lie on a line
A moderate linear trend: $y$ tends to fall as $x$ rises

items.q: A student says, "The curved plot has $r = 0.04$, so $x$ and $y$ are unrelated." What should you tell the student?

options: A strong curve can have $r$ near 0, as this plot shows.
Squaring a small number makes it smaller and still ignores the curve.
It is correct; the arch is symmetric, so the upward and downward halves cancel in $r$.
Right: always plot the data; a near-zero $r$ rules out only a linear pattern.
The student is right: a correlation near 0 means no relationship of any kind
The student should square $r$ to see the true strength
The correlation was probably computed wrong
Look at the plot first: $r$ misses curved relationships

items.q: Across cities, the number of fire trucks sent to a fire and the dollar damage have a correlation of 0.7. What explains this best?

why.correct: A strong correlation can come from a lurking variable.
options: $r$ is not a percent of anything.
Right: fire size is a lurking variable linked to both. Correlation does not mean the trucks cause damage.
The correlation is real; its explanation is a lurking variable.
Correlation is not causation; a third variable explains both.
70% of the damage is caused by the trucks
Bigger fires bring more trucks and more damage
The correlation is probably a mistake in the data
The fire trucks themselves cause most of the damage

items.q: Which correlation shows the strongest linear association?

options: That is weak.
That is weak.
Size 0.70 is smaller than 0.85.
Right: its size, 0.85, is the largest.

items.q: Which statement about the correlation $r$ is true?

options: A strong curve can give $r$ near 0.
$r = 1$ only when the points lie exactly on a rising line.
Right: it is computed from z-scores, which have no units.
That describes a slope.
It is large for any strong curved pattern
It is 1 whenever $y$ increases with $x$
It is between $-1$ and 1 and has no units
It is measured in the units of $y$ per unit of $x$

items.q: Five students have these products of z-scores, $z_x z_y$: 1.1, 0.6, 0.2, 0.7 and 1.0. Write the expression for the correlation $r = \frac{1}{n - 1}\sum z_x z_y$, then give its value.

mistakes.why: Divide by $n - 1 = 4$, as for a standard deviation, not by $n = 5$.
The sum alone is 3.6, which cannot be a correlation. Divide it by $n - 1$.

items.q: Why does a point in the upper right of a scatterplot (above average on both variables) push $r$ up?

why.correct: Upper right and lower left: positive products; upper left and lower right: negative.
options: Distance from the origin does not matter; what matters is position relative to the means.
Raw size does not matter, since $r$ uses standardized values.
Every point counts once.
Right: $r$ averages $z_x z_y$; points in the upper right and lower left give positive products.
It is far from the origin, and distance from the origin raises $r$
It has large raw values, and $r$ grows with the size of the values
Points in the upper right count twice in the formula
Its two z-scores are positive, so their product is positive

items.q: A study of 1,000 adults finds $r = 0.45$ between hours of TV and weight. A headline says, "TV makes you gain weight." What is the main problem?

options: Right: this is observational, so a cause cannot be claimed.
A thousand adults is plenty. The design, not the size, is the problem.
A moderate correlation can be real; the problem is the causal claim.
That is not what $r$ means, and the headline's problem is about cause.
It is observational; other variables, like exercise, could explain it
The sample of 1,000 adults is too small to trust
A correlation of 0.45 is too small to mean anything
$r = 0.45$ means TV explains 45% of weight
